title: Reviewing your Games Day 2!
reviewNotes: All 66 saved states and captions reviewed. This follower-game review is an opening/middlegame lesson about the central ...e4 trap, f3 weakening, counting attackers and missing ...Qf2 mate. The clip ends in that early queen/knight attack with many pieces and pawns still present. There is no worked endgame setup or conversion. Retained in the searchable channel archive rather than the endgame-study queue.
transcript: This is day two of reviewing my followers games every day until I reach 100,000 followers. If you want me to review your game, all you have to do is follow me, like this video, and comment your chess.com username. Mohawk writes, "I'm rated 150, and I even know how to sacrifice pieces. I have many brilliant moves, but I don't know why my Elo isn't going up. I need an advice." Well, Mohawk, here is your game. You were playing white, and you started with E4 and developed your knight. All of this is good. And then your opponent goes for a very weird central attack. You correctly take the pawn, but now we need to know what happens after E4. This is the whole idea of this opening. We're trying to dislodge the white pawn to attack the white knight. If you are an E4 player, you need to know what to do against this kind of traps. Because at this rating range, a lot of people play traps. In this case, the best move is queen to E2, pinning the pawn to the king. And now, for example, if black picks up this pawn, they lose on the spot after knight to C3 attacking the queen and the pawn. You're going to win back the pawn and have a pretty good initiative. Instead, you jump to the center, and this allows black to capture the pawn back with a tempo on the knight. This means that you are already forced to defend this knight. Now, you defend the knight with a pawn. I don't love this, simply because in the future this knight can always get kicked away by the C pawn anyway. So, we might as well move it, for example, to B3, where it's a little bit more safe. And your next move is quite weakening. You play F3. Grandmaster Ben Finegold always says, "Never push the F pawn." And the reason why is that we are opening this diagonal to the king. Your opponent puts pressure on the knight. You take. This is okay. I would suggest you cover with the queen. You have to ask yourself, "Whose queen is strongest in this position?" And it is very obvious that the black queen is far more stronger than this white queen. So, we would be happy with a queen trade. If black takes, we bring back the knight, and we are ready to push in the center, and we're fine. But instead, you cover with the knight, and now you get [music] punished right away for opening this diagonal. If black goes queen to H4 check, you either cover with the G pawn and lose your rook right away, or if you cover with the knight, now your king is completely exposed, and notice that you cannot castle again because you opened up the F pawn. Instead, your opponent tries to put pressure some different ways. They blunder a piece, so now you're happy. All of a sudden, you're completely winning, but you blunder a piece back. Now, a very simple way to make sure that you're not blundering pieces is to count the defenders and the attackers. Here there are two attackers, one and two, and there's only one defender. So, of course, if black takes, you're just losing a bishop. Now, here you're completely winning, but you need to ask yourself, especially when you have two pieces so close to your king, are there any threats? And the way that you look for threats is starting by looking at the checks, and that's how we see the move queen to F2, which is going to be a checkmate in one move. In only 13 seconds, you play this bishop move, and you get checkmated in one move. So, my advice for you is this. It's good that you can find brilliant moves, but remember that chess games are more often won by outsmarting your opponent strategically. So, you need to work on your understanding of the opening principles, and in general, be prepared against these traps.
